subject: Human Factors
title: Medical eligibility and fitness today
text: Human Factors Medical eligibility and fitness today A medical certificate documents an eligibility determination. It does not guarantee that you are fit for every flight during its validity. Illness, medication, poor sleep, stress, alcohol, and dehydration can change performance between examinations. Use IMSAFE to discuss those personal factors, then use PAVE to consider the pilot, aircraft, environment, and external pressures together. An Aviation Medical Examiner handles medical examinations through the FAA process. A special issuance may permit certification with a condition requiring additional evaluation or monitoring. A Statement of Demonstrated Ability addresses certain stable conditions through demonstrated capability. Neither is permission to ignore new symptoms. The applicable medical or alternative qualification depends on the operation and the pilot’s eligibility. Why it matters: medical qualification and self-assessment solve different problems. The examination is periodic; operational risk changes continuously. A pilot may meet a minimum legal requirement while lacking adequate alertness for turbulence, unfamiliar airspace, or a demanding approach. When a condition or medication creates uncertainty, obtain aviation-medical advice before flying. A passenger’s schedule does not restore physiological reserve. Apply it: change the departure, use another pilot, simplify the flight, or cancel before fatigue becomes an airborne problem. A pilot holds a valid medical certificate but slept three hours and feels unable to concentrate. Which decision best addresses the actual risk?

subject: Human Factors
title: Hypoxia, breathing, and carbon monoxide
text: Human Factors Hypoxia, breathing, and carbon monoxide Hypoxia means inadequate oxygen at the tissues. Hypoxic hypoxia begins with insufficient oxygen pressure available to the lungs. Hypemic hypoxia limits blood carriage, as with carbon monoxide exposure. Stagnant hypoxia limits circulation. Histotoxic hypoxia prevents cells from using available oxygen effectively. The oxygen percentage in ordinary air remains roughly constant with altitude, while its partial pressure falls. Headache, impaired judgment, unusual confidence, slowed responses, or visual deterioration deserve action; a person may feel well while performing poorly. Hyperventilation has a different mechanism: breathing removes carbon dioxide faster than the body produces it. Tingling and lightheadedness can resemble hypoxia. Do not diagnose uncertain symptoms by removing oxygen. At altitude, use the appropriate oxygen equipment, verify delivery, control breathing, and arrange a safe descent according to the aircraft procedures and situation. Carbon monoxide is colorless and odorless; cabin heat may introduce exhaust contamination after a system failure. Follow the aircraft emergency procedure, obtain fresh air, use oxygen if available, land promptly, and obtain medical evaluation. A routine pulse oximeter can be misleading during carbon monoxide exposure. The useful distinction is where oxygen delivery fails, because simply increasing cabin airflow does not correct every cause. At altitude a pilot is breathing rapidly, feels tingling, and has trouble reasoning. Why is simply shutting off oxygen an unsafe response?

subject: Human Factors
title: Pressure changes, sickness, and physical reserve
text: Human Factors Pressure changes, sickness, and physical reserve As outside pressure falls in a climb, trapped gas expands. During descent, increasing pressure requires the middle ear and sinuses to equalize. A cold or nasal inflammation may obstruct that process. Pain is a warning, and forcing the issue through a rapid descent can worsen injury. Prevention and sound medical advice are more dependable than trying an unfamiliar decongestant before departure. Motion sickness arises from conflicting sensory information. A student may first become quiet, pale, or inattentive. Reduce workload, provide ventilation, shorten the lesson, and land when appropriate. Fatigue, heat, dehydration, and sustained stress further reduce the attention available for flying. After scuba diving: dissolved nitrogen can form bubbles when pressure decreases. FAA guidance recommends at least 12 hours before flight to actual altitudes up to 8,000 feet after a dive not requiring decompression stops, and at least 24 hours after a dive requiring them. subject: Human Factors
title: Why your senses can disagree
text: Human Factors Why your senses can disagree The inner ear detects accelerations well but is a poor long-term attitude reference without reliable visual cues. A slow bank can go unnoticed; rolling level may then feel like a bank the other way. Moving the head during a sustained turn can create a powerful false tumbling sensation. Acceleration may feel like pitching up, tempting an unsafe nose-down input. The eyes also need interpretation. Sloping clouds can become a false horizon. A narrow runway or an upsloping runway can make the aircraft seem higher than it is. Featureless dark terrain removes familiar approach-height cues. An isolated light may seem to wander when stared at for a long time. Why: the brain combines several imperfect signals rather than measuring attitude directly. When a familiar cue disappears, confidence in the remaining sensation may increase even while accuracy decreases. Use a disciplined instrument cross-check when external references are unreliable. An instrument-qualified pilot must still remain proficient; instruments cannot help if they are ignored or misread. Teach it: ask the student to describe the instrument indications that would distinguish an actual climb from a false pitch-up sensation. subject: Human Factors
title: Attention, bias, and practical decisions
text: Human Factors Attention, bias, and practical decisions Attention is limited. A minor radio problem can absorb enough of it to cause a major flight-path error. First keep the airplane controlled, then establish a safe navigation plan, and communicate as workload permits. Use available resources: ATC, another qualified pilot, an autopilot used correctly, a diversion airport, or simply more time. Expectation bias means perceiving what you expected. Confirmation bias means favoring information that supports an existing belief. Hearing one traffic call and seeing one airplane does not prove they refer to the same aircraft. Deliberately seek a second check: position, altitude, direction, distance, or a repeated instruction. A usable decision cycle is to detect the change, assess its significance, choose an outcome, act, and reassess. PAVE helps identify risks; it does not produce a numerical permission slip. Hazardous attitudes also need an actionable correction: slow down impulsive decisions, reject the idea that experience prevents accidents, accept useful rules, and remember that changing a plan is an available action. Scenario: deteriorating visibility plus fuel uncertainty and a waiting passenger is a combined problem. A timely diversion can remove several pressures at once. Waiting for each individual risk to reach a legal limit can eliminate the remaining options. You hear an aircraft report final and see a different aircraft farther out. subject: Human Factors
title: Instructor habits, alcohol, and medication
text: Human Factors Instructor habits, alcohol, and medication Make control ownership explicit with a positive exchange and visual confirmation. During taxi, runway operations, and other high-workload phases, keep conversation relevant to the task. The instructor must protect the flight while teaching; two people looking down at the same display do not provide two independent safety checks. Under 14 CFR 91.17, a crewmember may not act or attempt to act within eight hours after drinking, while under the influence, while using an impairing drug, or with an alcohol concentration 0.04 or greater . Passing eight hours or having a lower concentration does not override impairment. Prescription status does not make a medication compatible with flying. Training application: introduce distractions progressively and deliberately, with a clear safety margin. Evaluate whether the learner recognizes the distraction and postpones a lower-priority task. Avoid demonstrations that create a real loss of control or runway hazard merely to prove a point. The passenger provision in 91.17 has an emergency exception and distinguishes a medical patient under proper care. Teach the actual rule rather than an absolute prohibition stripped of its exceptions. For medication, consider the underlying condition, side effects, interactions, and FAA medical guidance together; do not suggest stopping prescribed treatment without the treating clinician. subject: Visual Scanning and Collision Avoidance
title: Why a continuous glance misses traffic
text: Visual Scanning and Collision Avoidance Why a continuous glance misses traffic Sharp daylight detail occupies a small part of the visual field. Sweeping the eyes rapidly across the entire windscreen gives a feeling of coverage without allowing enough time to detect a small aircraft. Scan successive sectors with deliberate pauses, looking above and below the horizon as well as along it. Move the head to see around a windshield post. The retinal center is cone-rich and suited to daylight detail and color. Rods away from the center are more sensitive in darkness. At night, slightly off-center viewing can reveal a dim target lost when stared at directly. The optic-nerve blind spot is a separate anatomical limitation; it is not the same as the night blind spot. Why: detection requires contrast, a useful focus, and enough viewing time. Fatigue, hypoxia, glare, dirty transparencies, haze, and frequent near-to-far refocusing all reduce the margin. In an empty or hazy field, the eyes may relax to an unhelpfully near distance. Deliberately refocus on distant features, then resume the scan. Use suitable eye protection and cockpit lighting without sacrificing the ability to see relevant displays. FAA scanning guidance suggests short movements no larger than about ten degrees and observing each area for at least a second. Treat that as a technique to practice, not an assurance that a completed scan found everything. During a hazy practice-area flight, the student stares far ahead continuously but misses nearby traffic. Which change best improves the scan?

subject: Visual Scanning and Collision Avoidance
title: The collision target may look stationary
text: Visual Scanning and Collision Avoidance The collision target may look stationary An airplane on a collision course can remain near the same place on your windscreen while its image becomes larger. Little relative angular motion is a warning, not reassurance. An aircraft whose bearing moves may still be a threat if its path or altitude changes. Keep tracking the encounter and create separation early. Closure combines the motion of both aircraft. Two aircraft approaching head-on at 120 knots each close at 240 knots: four nautical miles per minute. From one nautical mile apart, only 15 seconds remain if both continue unchanged. Detection, recognition, choosing an action, and aircraft response all consume that time. Why: in a simple constant-velocity collision geometry, the relative-position vector stays pointed in the same direction while its length shrinks. The target therefore appears almost motionless until late in the encounter, when its angular size grows rapidly. This explains why scanning only for obvious movement is unreliable. Apply it: describe traffic by position, altitude, movement, and distance, and establish clear control ownership if action is required. Do not allow a student’s search to become a prolonged fixation on one sector. Maintain aircraft control and a broad traffic picture while making the appropriate avoidance maneuver. A small aircraft remains at nearly the same place on the windscreen and grows larger. What does that suggest? Two aircraft fly directly toward each other at 120 knots each. They are one nautical mile apart. Assuming unchanged speeds and paths, how long until their positions coincide?

subject: Visual Scanning and Collision Avoidance
title: Clearing is an ongoing process
text: Visual Scanning and Collision Avoidance Clearing is an ongoing process Clear the intended flight path before turns, climbs, descents, and maneuvers. Aircraft structure changes which areas are hidden: a high wing can hide the inside of a turn or traffic above; a low wing can hide traffic below. Move the aircraft and your head appropriately to reveal those areas while remaining within a safe, planned flight path. A pair of clearing turns may be a useful local training procedure, but there is no universal rule that exactly two 90-degree turns guarantee a clear practice area. The scan must continue during the maneuver. Verbal calls such as “clear left” should reflect an actual look rather than a memorized response. Apply it: before rolling into a left turn in a high-wing trainer, briefly reveal and inspect the area the wing would otherwise cover. During climbs and descents, use appropriate clearing techniques rather than holding a blind attitude indefinitely. Avoid descending into a traffic pattern without checking traffic at the entry altitude. A clearance from ATC does not prove the runway or approach is physically clear. Scan the approach areas before runway entry and the runway environment before landing. If a threat conflicts with an instruction, maintain safety and promptly advise ATC rather than assuming someone else has already resolved it. subject: Visual Scanning and Collision Avoidance
title: Predictability and right of way
text: Visual Scanning and Collision Avoidance Predictability and right of way Under 91.113, when weather permits, pilots operating under IFR as well as VFR must remain vigilant to see and avoid other aircraft. ATC separation responsibilities vary with airspace and services; receiving a clearance or flight following does not remove the pilot’s visual responsibility. For a head-on encounter, each aircraft alters course to the right. For converging aircraft of the same category at approximately the same altitude, the aircraft with the other on its right yields. An overtaking aircraft stays clear and passes to the right. Other rules cover category priority, distress, and landing. Right of way is a framework for predictable action, not permission to continue into a collision. Why: a shared response convention reduces the chance that two pilots choose conflicting avoidance actions. Predictable pattern entries and published traffic directions similarly reduce uncertainty near an airport. An aircraft at a lower altitude on approach has landing priority subject to the rule’s limitations; it may not exploit that position to cut in front of another aircraft on final or overtake it. Use the actual regulation and airport publications when teaching exceptions and local procedures. A radio announcement broadcasts an intention. It does not reserve airspace, establish a runway clearance at a non-towered airport, or change an existing right-of-way obligation. subject: Visual Scanning and Collision Avoidance
title: Traffic displays, ATC, radios, and lighting
text: Visual Scanning and Collision Avoidance Traffic displays, ATC, radios, and lighting ADS-B In, radar traffic advisories, CTAF calls, aircraft lights, and a second set of eyes can help aim your scan. Each adds information with limits. A display may omit unequipped aircraft, contain delayed reports, or show a target whose altitude or position is uncertain. Absence of a symbol does not establish an empty sky. ATC clock-position traffic calls generally refer to the aircraft’s observed ground track rather than a measured cockpit heading. A crosswind can therefore shift the expected visual direction. Confirm the traffic call’s altitude, distance, and direction of travel. “Traffic in sight” should identify the correct target, not simply any airplane nearby. Why: safety layers are most useful when their failure modes differ. A clean windscreen and a systematic outside scan address visual detection. A radio report helps build a traffic model. A display helps locate an equipped target. Those tools fail differently, so combining them is better than substituting one for all the others. Ask passengers to report traffic with a simple clock position and relative height. Use lighting appropriate to the aircraft and situation; bright strobes in cloud or near other pilots can impair rather than improve visibility. Synthetic vision depicts modeled terrain and obstacles; it does not make unseen aircraft disappear. ATC reports traffic at your two o’clock, but a strong crosswind creates a large crab angle. subject: Visual Scanning and Collision Avoidance
title: Where to expect concentrated risk
text: Visual Scanning and Collision Avoidance Where to expect concentrated risk Traffic converges near airports, final approaches, common practice areas, navigation fixes, and popular routes. Good visibility can increase the number of aircraft in those areas while making pilots less suspicious of risk. Watch for an aircraft descending onto a high-wing airplane from above or a low-wing aircraft hiding traffic beneath it. Before a lesson, choose an area, altitude plan, escape direction, and division of scanning responsibility. Keep heads-down programming brief and deliberate. If the area becomes crowded, move or defer a maneuver rather than trying to complete the lesson inside an inadequate margin. Teach it: have the student identify likely conflicts from an airport diagram and the planned practice-area route. Then ask what a radio or display would miss. Evaluate how the student resumes a full scan after locating one reported aircraft. A useful standard is observable behavior: the learner checks aircraft blind spots, keeps flight-path control during a search, reports a specific target accurately, and acts before the encounter becomes urgent. Repeatedly asking “do you see it?” without defining who is flying or which sector to inspect can consume the very attention needed for avoidance.

subject: Runway Incursion Avoidance
title: The protected area and the whole airplane
text: Runway Incursion Avoidance The protected area and the whole airplane A runway incursion involves an incorrect presence of an aircraft, vehicle, or person in the protected area used for landing and takeoff. The hazard extends beyond an aircraft sitting on the painted runway surface. A wingtip or tail extending across a holding boundary can intrude while the cockpit appears clear. Before taxi, locate the departure runway, expected route, crossings, and published hot spots on a current airport diagram. A hot spot flags a place with a history or potential for confusion or collision; it is a reason to prepare for the specific geometry, not a separate clearance. Know how a runway change would alter the plan. Why: the pilot sees from one point in an aircraft with a large footprint. Holding-position markings and protected areas preserve space for arriving or departing traffic, including wing and obstacle clearance. Treat the airplane’s position as a physical envelope rather than the location of the nosewheel or a moving-map dot. Scenario: the next intersection looks familiar, but its sign differs from the diagram you expected. Stop where safe before entering an uncertain area. Ask for clarification or progressive taxi instructions. Continuing a few more feet to discover where you are can consume the protected separation you were trying to preserve. You reach an unfamiliar intersection and cannot reconcile the sign with the taxi diagram. What should happen before entering the uncertain area?

subject: Runway Incursion Avoidance
title: Signs, markings, and lighting as cross-checks
text: Runway Incursion Avoidance Signs, markings, and lighting as cross-checks A runway holding-position marking has two solid and two dashed yellow lines. Approaching from the solid side, remain behind it until authorized to enter or cross at an airport with an operating tower. Stop so that no part of the airplane extends past the boundary. A runway hold sign uses white characters on red. A taxiway location sign has a black background with yellow identification; direction signs use yellow with black information. Use the sign, pavement marking, diagram, and surrounding geometry together. A single clue is less reliable in darkness, rain, glare, or construction. Yellow guard lights draw attention to a runway boundary. They do not supply a clearance. Why: independent visual cues reduce the risk of recognizing the right shape at the wrong location. A runway number can be checked against a heading indication before departure, but magnetic indication alone does not prove the correct parallel runway. Verify the full runway designation and the actual pavement. The dashed side generally faces the runway being exited. Crossing that boundary while leaving the landing runway is different from crossing another runway ahead. An ILS critical-area hold marking and an intersecting-taxiway hold marking have different designs and purposes. Learn each as a distinct instruction rather than labeling every yellow line “the runway.”

subject: Runway Incursion Avoidance
title: A taxi route does not authorize every runway movement
text: Runway Incursion Avoidance A taxi route does not authorize every runway movement A taxi instruction identifies a destination and route. It does not by itself authorize entering the departure runway or crossing every intervening runway. Obtain explicit permission for each runway crossing and for runway entry. A clearance to cross a runway is not a takeoff clearance. Line up and wait permits positioning on the specified runway and waiting; it does not permit beginning the takeoff roll. Write the clearance, identify each limit on the diagram, and read back runway assignments, runway crossings, and hold-short instructions with the aircraft identification. Listen for the controller’s correction. If the transmission is incomplete, blocked, or ambiguous, ask again before moving into the uncertain area. Why: errors often begin when a pilot hears the expected route rather than the actual instruction. Reading back while locating each named taxiway checks both memory and interpretation. At a boundary, compare the instruction you actually received against the sign immediately in front of you. Practice: give the learner a changed route with an intermediate hold short. Ask the learner to point to the limit and explain what further authorization would be needed. Do not reward a fast readback if the student cannot locate the clearance boundary. If an instruction appears unsafe or conflicts with a visible hazard, communicate the conflict promptly. Ground assigns a route to Runway 27 that crosses Runway 18, but no crossing authorization is heard. What should the pilot do at Runway 18? Tower instructs the aircraft to line up and wait. The runway ahead looks clear. Which action is authorized?
summary: A taxi instruction identifies a destination and route. It does not by itself authorize entering the departure runway or crossing every intervening run

subject: Runway Incursion Avoidance
title: Taxi workload and non-towered operations
text: Runway Incursion Avoidance Taxi workload and non-towered operations Taxi is an active flight-safety task. Finish programming and lengthy checklist discussion while stopped in a suitable place. Keep the cockpit focused on movement, traffic, routing, and instructions. Brief passengers before taxi so that a request for quiet during a busy intersection is expected rather than abrupt. At a non-towered airport, no ground controller supplies runway separation or authorizes your crossing. Review the airport information and traffic direction, monitor the appropriate frequency, announce relevant intentions, and visually check the runway and approach areas before entering. Radio silence and a self-announcement are both insufficient proof that the runway is safe. Why: taxi combines steering, braking, clearance interpretation, radio monitoring, and an unfamiliar visual scene. A moving map can help orientation, but heads-down fixation and inaccurate position display can create a new hazard. Maintain enough speed margin to stop before a hold boundary, obstacle, or developing conflict. At an airport with a closed tower, confirm the published procedures and airspace status rather than assuming daytime tower procedures still apply. Teach the student to state what evidence supports a runway entry: known position, a suitable traffic picture, visual checks, and compliance with the applicable procedures. A transmission reports intent; it does not force other traffic to yield. At a non-towered airport, the frequency is quiet after your departure announcement. What does that establish?

subject: Runway Incursion Avoidance
title: The runway is not clear until the tail is clear
text: Runway Incursion Avoidance The runway is not clear until the tail is clear Before landing, brief likely exits and any adjacent runway. After landing, maintain control and clear the landing runway using an appropriate exit. The aircraft is not clear until all parts are beyond its applicable holding-position marking. Crossing that marking must not carry the aircraft into another runway’s protected area without the required authorization. Once safely clear, obtain or follow the applicable taxi instruction. Avoid stopping on the runway to change frequencies or perform an after-landing checklist. Equally, do not accept a hurried exit that exceeds safe turning or braking capability. If there is insufficient space between boundaries, tell ATC rather than guessing which runway area may be occupied. LAHSO: land-and-hold-short operations require the pilot to understand the stopping point and available landing distance, assess actual performance, and explicitly accept or decline the clearance. The FAA advises student pilots and pilots unfamiliar with LAHSO not to participate. A pilot may decline an unsafe or unsuitable offer. Why: after touchdown, workload falls just as vigilance often relaxes. Nearby parallel or intersecting runways make a successful landing followed by a wrong turn entirely possible. Continue the positional cross-check until parking, including the location of the entire aircraft and each remaining clearance limit. The nosewheel has crossed a runway exit holding-position marking, but the tail has not. Is the aircraft clear of the landing runway?

subject: Runway Incursion Avoidance
title: Night, low visibility, and runway status lights
text: Runway Incursion Avoidance Night, low visibility, and runway status lights Darkness and poor visibility reduce the distance at which signs, painted lines, and vehicles can be recognized. Taxi more slowly as needed, use an airport diagram, and identify a boundary early enough to stop. Lighting patterns help orientation, but a blue edge light or green centerline alone does not establish which taxiway you occupy. Avoid lighting that blinds another pilot or obscures your own view. Runway status lights independently warn of detected conflicts. Illuminated red runway entrance or takeoff hold lights mean an unsafe condition exists. Remain stopped or stop safely as appropriate, and advise ATC when the indication conflicts with an instruction. Why: the surveillance-based warning is a safety layer separate from the controller’s clearance. The controller may not be able to see the activation directly. Lights going out do not authorize entry, crossing, or takeoff; the applicable ATC clearance is still required. If already in a dynamic situation where stopping would itself be unsafe, use the safest aircraft-specific judgment and communicate promptly. Do not turn a simple “red means stop” teaching model into a demand for an unsafe high-speed action. The learner should understand both the warning’s meaning and the need to manage the actual aircraft state. subject: Principles of Flight
title: Forces, airflow, and lift production
text: Principles of Flight Forces, airflow, and lift production Weight acts toward Earth. Aerodynamic lift is defined perpendicular to the relative airflow, while drag acts opposite the aircraft’s motion through that airflow. Lift is not defined perpendicular to the chord line and does not always point vertically upward. Thrust generally acts near the propeller or engine axis. In steady, unaccelerated flight, the vector sum of the forces is zero even during a steady climb or descent. A wing turns airflow and produces a pressure distribution around its surfaces. The pressure forces on the wing and the momentum change in the air describe the same interaction. Bernoulli’s relationship and Newton’s laws are compatible descriptions; the air divided at the leading edge has no requirement to reunite at the trailing edge. The useful equation: lift equals dynamic pressure times wing area times lift coefficient. Here V is speed relative to the air, not groundspeed. Shape, angle of attack, configuration, and flow conditions influence Cₗ. A cambered airfoil can make positive lift at zero geometric angle of attack. More speed or wing area can increase lift without changing that geometric angle. L = 1 2 ρ V 2 S C L In a simple steady climb with thrust aligned with the flight path, part of weight acts along the path and lift balances the perpendicular component. “Climbing means lift is greater than weight” is therefore an unreliable general explanation. A cambered airfoil produces positive lift at zero geometric angle of attack. Which explanation is consistent with aerodynamic principles?

subject: Principles of Flight
title: Angle of attack, separation, and stall
text: Principles of Flight Angle of attack, separation, and stall Angle of attack is the angle between an airfoil’s chord reference and the relative airflow. It is different from pitch attitude, which compares the aircraft with the horizon. A wing can reach its critical angle with a high or low nose attitude and at many airspeeds. As angle of attack rises, lift coefficient generally increases until the wing reaches its maximum usable coefficient. Extensive flow separation then reduces lift capability and increases drag. A stalled wing still produces aerodynamic force; it has not suddenly lost all lift. Recovery requires reducing angle of attack below the critical value, with the remaining actions and limitations taken from the aircraft procedures. Why indicated stall speed varies: speed is the amount of airflow needed to produce the required lift with the available maximum coefficient. Higher weight or load requires more lift and therefore more speed at that limit. Flaps, contamination, or a changed wing shape can change both the lift curve and the critical angle. A universal critical angle such as “16 degrees for every airplane” is not a valid operational limit. Flaps often increase maximum lift coefficient and reduce stall speed, even if the geometric angle at stall decreases. Ice can degrade the curve and warning margin in ways a clean-wing demonstration does not predict. During an aerodynamic stall, which change is essential to restore attached-flow capability?

title: Drag and the energy required to climb
text: Principles of Flight Drag and the energy required to climb Parasite drag includes shape, skin-friction, and interference effects. At otherwise fixed conditions, it rises strongly as airspeed increases. Induced drag is associated with producing lift with a finite wing. For a fixed lift requirement, lower speed requires a larger lift coefficient and usually more induced drag. Combining those trends produces a minimum-drag region. A sustainable climb needs energy in excess of that used to overcome drag. Raising the nose can initially trade kinetic energy for altitude, but that exchange cannot sustain the climb indefinitely. Power is the rate of energy transfer: the speed for maximum excess power produces the best rate of climb, while maximum excess thrust relates to best climb angle. Ground effect changes the wing’s induced-flow pattern and can reduce induced drag near the surface. It does not create energy. subject: Principles of Flight
title: Bank, load factor, and the flight envelope
text: Principles of Flight Bank, load factor, and the flight envelope In a coordinated, constant-altitude turn, the vertical component of lift must still balance weight. Banking directs another component inward to curve the flight path. Total lift must therefore increase. The ratio L/W is load factor, n. For this specific model, the load factor is the reciprocal of the cosine of bank. At 60 degrees, n = 2: total lift is twice weight. n = L W = 1 cos φ V S n = V S 1 n With weight, configuration, and maximum lift coefficient fixed, stall speed rises as the square root of load factor. A 50-knot one-g stall speed becomes about 71 knots at two g. Bank alone does not impose that load in every maneuver; unloading or allowing a descent changes the force requirement. Why the envelope matters: a V–g diagram combines aerodynamic stall boundaries with structural load and speed limits. At high speed, a sharp control input may reach a structural limit before a protective stall occurs. At low speed, an accelerated stall can occur well above the familiar one-g stall speed. Use the actual AFM/POH category, loading restrictions, maneuvering speeds, and limitations. Historical normal- and utility-category figures are examples, not universal permissions. Ultimate load is a certification-strength margin beyond limit load, not an extra pilot operating allowance. Maneuvering speed also does not protect against every gust, repeated control input, or combined-axis loading. In a coordinated, constant-altitude 60-degree bank, an aircraft has a 50-knot one-g stall speed. With configuration and weight unchanged, what is the approximate two-g stall speed, rounded to the nearest knot?

subject: Principles of Flight
title: Static stability, damping, and center of gravity
text: Principles of Flight Static stability, damping, and center of gravity Static stability describes the initial response to a disturbance: toward the original condition, no restoring tendency, or farther away. Dynamic stability describes what happens over time. A response can initially restore but still oscillate with increasing amplitude. Positive damping removes energy from the oscillation; neutral damping sustains it and negative damping increases it. Pitch stability depends on the whole aircraft, including the wing, tail, fuselage, downwash, power, and center of gravity. Moving the CG aft generally reduces the restoring pitch tendency and changes control-force and recovery margins. Moving it forward can increase the tail force and control authority required for takeoff and landing. A better deeper model: compare CG with the aircraft’s neutral point, rather than treating a moving “center of lift” as a universal hinge. A conventional aircraft often uses a downward tail force in a particular trimmed condition, but that is not a universal rule for every configuration and maneuver. Dihedral and related geometry couple sideslip into roll; the vertical tail provides directional restoring effects. These mechanisms do not guarantee that every roll–yaw mode is well damped. Remaining inside the approved CG envelope protects the tested balance of stability and control. “Aft CG is always unrecoverable” overstates the issue; the serious concern is the reduced margin and potentially inadequate recovery outside approved limits. Moving the CG aft toward the whole-aircraft neutral point generally has which effect?

subject: Principles of Flight
title: Why propeller effects change with the maneuver
text: Principles of Flight Why propeller effects change with the maneuver For a typical clockwise-turning propeller viewed from the cockpit, torque reaction tends to roll the aircraft left. Spiraling slipstream can strike the vertical tail and yaw the nose left. At a positive angle between propeller axis and relative airflow, unequal blade loading can shift thrust toward the descending side of the disc, creating P-factor yaw. A spinning propeller also has angular momentum. Changing the orientation of that rotating system creates gyroscopic effects whose direction depends on propeller rotation and the applied pitch or yaw change. A tailwheel airplane raising its tail is a useful example, but a memorized “always left” rule cannot describe every maneuver or opposite-rotating propeller. Why power and airspeed matter: high power increases propeller-related forces while low airspeed can reduce the effectiveness of aerodynamic controls. A nose-high, high-power climb can therefore need more coordination input than cruise. The correct input is the amount that produces the required aircraft response, not a fixed pedal position recalled from another flight. The rudder counters yaw and manages sideslip; the ailerons primarily control roll. Avoid explaining torque roll as though the rudder directly cancels an equal roll moment. Aircraft rigging, trim, propeller direction, and the current maneuver determine how those effects combine. Teach the causes separately before discussing their combined cockpit symptoms.

subject: Principles of Flight
title: Wake turbulence and the limits of prediction
text: Principles of Flight Wake turbulence and the limits of prediction A finite wing producing lift leaves a rotating wake. The strongest hazardous wakes are associated with heavy, clean, slow aircraft. A following light aircraft may not have enough roll control to oppose an encounter. Vortices initially descend and can drift with the wind; near the ground they can spread laterally. A light crosswind may keep one vortex near the runway while moving the other away. Plan avoidance around the preceding aircraft’s actual flight path, rotation point, touchdown point, wind, and the available runway. In suitable same-runway situations, staying above its approach path and landing beyond its touchdown, or rotating before its rotation point and climbing above its path, can help. Why those rules need judgment: the preceding path may be unknown, an intersecting runway may produce a different encounter, and the following aircraft may not be able to outclimb the leader. Wake does not follow a perfectly timed elevator down through the air. Terrain, wind shear, atmospheric conditions, and aircraft behavior change its location and persistence. Request more spacing or delay when the avoidance geometry is uncertain. Comply with applicable separation requirements, but do not assume that the passage of a minimum interval proves the wake is gone. Wake is linked to lift production, not solely to aircraft engine operation or the sound of a departing jet. A light airplane follows a heavy, clean aircraft on final with a light crosswind. Which plan best reflects wake uncertainty?

subject: Aircraft Flight Controls and Operation of Systems
title: Axes, control surfaces, and coordination
text: Aircraft Flight Controls and Operation of Systems Axes, control surfaces, and coordination Ailerons primarily command roll about the longitudinal axis. Elevator or stabilator input changes pitching moment about the lateral axis. Rudder primarily commands yaw about the vertical axis. The flight path changes through the resulting forces; a pitch input is not a direct promise of climb, and yaw alone is not the normal way to generate a coordinated turn. During roll entry, asymmetric wing drag can yaw the nose opposite the intended bank. Appropriate rudder coordinates the maneuver. In an established turn, control requirements change with aircraft characteristics and flight condition. Watch the airplane’s response rather than applying the same pedal position from entry through rollout. Why the rudder has more than one job: it manages yaw and sideslip during turns, but also supports crosswind control, intentional slips, asymmetric-thrust handling, and some recovery procedures. A slip can be deliberate and useful when allowed by the aircraft procedures; it is not automatically an error. A skid near a stall is a different and potentially serious condition. Use the inclinometer and outside picture appropriately. A centered ball is coordination information; the miniature aircraft in a conventional turn coordinator is principally rate information, not a substitute attitude indicator. Teach a light, controlled grip so the student can sense pressure changes without repeatedly overcorrecting.

subject: Aircraft Flight Controls and Operation of Systems
title: Trim, flaps, and secondary controls
text: Aircraft Flight Controls and Operation of Systems Trim, flaps, and secondary controls Trim relieves the sustained control force required for a chosen condition. Establish the desired attitude, power, and configuration, then remove the unwanted pressure. Re-trim when speed, power, or configuration changes. Trying to fly an entire correction with the trim wheel can delay control and hide an unsuitable flight condition. Flaps change wing geometry. They can increase maximum lift coefficient, reduce stall speed, add drag, and alter pitching moment. The balance varies with flap design and deflection. Slats and slots can delay separation by influencing the upper-surface flow. Spoilers reduce lift and often increase drag; their purposes and permitted use depend on the aircraft. Why a trim tab can move opposite the elevator: a conventional tab uses aerodynamic force on a small surface to create a balancing moment on the larger one. Other aircraft use stabilator anti-servo tabs, adjustable stabilizers, springs, or different mechanisms. Learn the installed design before predicting movement or failure behavior. Respect flap-extension speeds, configuration restrictions, and electric-trim/autopilot procedures. A ground-adjustable rudder tab is a rigging item, not an in-flight pilot control or an invitation to bend hardware casually. Obtain qualified maintenance guidance. The correct trim result is manageable control force, not hands-off proof that the aircraft will hold altitude indefinitely.

subject: Aircraft Flight Controls and Operation of Systems
title: Piston engines, ignition, and propellers
text: Aircraft Flight Controls and Operation of Systems Piston engines, ignition, and propellers A four-stroke reciprocating engine draws in a charge, compresses it, burns it to produce work, and expels exhaust. Many trainers use air-cooled, horizontally opposed engines with dual magneto ignition. A conventional magneto generates its own ignition energy, so loss of the aircraft alternator does not by itself stop that ignition. Electronically controlled or differently installed engines may have different dependencies. A fixed-pitch propeller has a blade-angle compromise; its rpm responds to power and flight condition. A constant-speed system uses a governor to vary blade pitch and maintain the selected rpm while it remains within the governing range. Blade stops and system limits prevent unlimited compensation. Why: each blade section is an airfoil. Its angle of attack depends on rotational speed, forward speed, and geometric pitch. If rpm tends to rise in a normal governing condition, the governor generally commands more blade loading by increasing pitch. If rpm tends to fall, it generally commands less. The exact oil-pressure and failure-to-pitch behavior depends on the installation. Use the aircraft’s approved sequence for power, propeller, and mixture changes. “Every C172 has the same engine” is false: model, serial range, modifications, and supplements matter. Identify the engine and propeller actually installed before teaching their normal and emergency procedures. title: Fuel, induction, oil, and supporting systems
text: Aircraft Flight Controls and Operation of Systems Fuel, induction, oil, and supporting systems Trace fuel from each tank through vents, selector, drains, pumps, metering, and injectors or carburetor. A high wing may provide gravity assistance, but that does not establish that every operating condition is independent of pumps or tank selection. Vent blockage, contamination, a wrong selector position, and an empty tank create different problems even when fuel remains elsewhere aboard. Carburetors and fuel-injection systems meter fuel differently. Carburetor icing can occur without visible structural ice; a fuel-injected engine avoids the carburetor’s particular icing mechanism but can still suffer induction blockage or other icing. Mixture management must follow the actual engine and POH guidance. Why oil matters: oil lubricates, carries heat, helps sealing, and carries contaminants to filtration or collection points. Depending on installation, it may also operate a propeller mechanism or other components. Pressure and temperature are related but distinct clues; neither should be dismissed because the other appears normal. Tank capacities, usable fuel, minimum oil, approved grades, pump operation, and hydraulic-fluid types are aircraft-specific. A 172R, 172S, older carbureted 172, or modified airplane need not match a slide’s figures. Use the approved systems description and limitations for that aircraft. subject: Aircraft Flight Controls and Operation of Systems
title: Electrical supply and shared failure paths
text: Aircraft Flight Controls and Operation of Systems Electrical supply and shared failure paths An alternator supplies electrical power and normally supports battery charging. The battery can provide starting energy and a limited reserve after a generating-system failure. A nominal 24-volt battery may operate in a nominal 28-volt charging system, but those labels are not universal aircraft specifications. The approved system voltage, alternator capacity, bus arrangement, and reserve duration come from the aircraft documentation. After an alternator failure, electrical equipment may appear normal initially because the battery is still supplying it. Follow the aircraft checklist to identify the problem, manage loads, and select a suitable landing plan. An illuminated display is not evidence that the charging system is healthy. Why redundancy needs a diagram: two displays may share a bus, sensor, antenna, or power source. A backup that fails from the same single cause is not fully independent. Conversely, a conventional magneto-powered engine can continue running while radios or electrically driven instruments lose their supply. Trace the installed autopilot’s power, attitude, air-data, trim, and disengagement paths. Know what its annunciations mean and how a failure changes control responsibility. subject: Aircraft Flight Controls and Operation of Systems
title: Pressure instruments and blockage patterns
text: Aircraft Flight Controls and Operation of Systems Pressure instruments and blockage patterns The airspeed indicator compares pitot total pressure with static pressure. Their difference relates to dynamic pressure and therefore airspeed. The altimeter senses static pressure using nearly evacuated aneroid elements and a calibrated mechanism. The altimeter setting adjusts the reference; the wafers are not simply containers permanently filled to 29.92 inches of mercury. A conventional vertical-speed indicator compares prompt static-pressure change with pressure delayed by a calibrated restriction. This shared plumbing explains shared symptoms. A blocked static source can freeze the altimeter, drive the VSI toward zero, and cause airspeed errors as altitude changes. A pitot blockage mainly affects the airspeed indication. Trace the trapped pressure: if the pitot inlet is blocked while its drain remains open, the airspeed reading normally falls toward zero. If both inlet and drain are blocked but static remains available, trapped pitot pressure can make the airspeed indication rise in a climb and fall in a descent. With static blocked and pitot clear, a climb above the blockage altitude generally makes the airspeed read too low. These are idealized diagnostic patterns, not a license to continue by mental correction. Use the installed alternate-static, pitot-heat, and unreliable-airspeed procedures. Cabin alternate-static pressure can differ from outside pressure, so apply the published corrections and limitations. title: Gyros, landing gear, and ice protection
text: Aircraft Flight Controls and Operation of Systems Gyros, landing gear, and ice protection Conventional attitude and heading gyros use rigidity in space; a turn-rate instrument uses gyroscopic response to rotation. Vacuum and electrical power sources vary by installation. Modern AHRS and electronic displays may replace the spinning gyros, but they still depend on sensors, power, and a validated attitude solution. subject: Performance and Limitations
title: Weight and balance: both limits matter
text: Performance and Limitations Weight and balance: both limits matter Weight is the total load. Balance describes where that load acts. An airplane can be below maximum weight and still have an unsafe center of gravity (CG). Both must remain inside the aircraft’s approved envelope throughout the planned flight, including after fuel burns. Use the aircraft’s current equipment list and weight-and-balance record. A sample handbook’s empty weight may differ from your airplane after repairs, equipment changes, or weighing. Basic empty weight normally includes installed equipment, unusable fuel, and operating fluids as defined for that aircraft. Useful load is the difference between the applicable maximum weight and basic empty weight. It must accommodate usable fuel, occupants, and baggage. Apply it: four seats do not establish a four-person payload. Check total weight, CG, baggage limits, seat limits, and the operating category required for the intended maneuvers. Think of CG as a weighted average, rather than a physical hinge. Each item contributes a moment equal to weight multiplied by its arm from the reference datum. Adding moments and dividing by total weight gives the loaded CG. The datum is a bookkeeping reference selected by the manufacturer; the airplane does not rotate around it in flight. Some manuals scale moments by 100 or 1,000. Keep the same scale throughout. Use the envelope’s actual horizontal axis: it may show inches, percent mean aerodynamic chord, or moment index. A correct arithmetic result plotted on the wrong chart is still an unsafe loading decision. A loading change remains below maximum gross weight but moves CG beyond the aft limit. What is the appropriate conclusion?

subject: Performance and Limitations
title: Calculate the effect of moving a load
text: Performance and Limitations Calculate the effect of moving a load Build the calculation in a consistent sequence: start with current empty weight and moment, add each load at its assigned arm, sum weights and moments, then divide total moment by total weight. Compare the resulting point with the correct envelope, not just a single maximum-weight number. For a load shifted within the aircraft, total weight stays constant. The change in moment is the shifted weight multiplied by the distance moved. Divide that moment change by the aircraft’s total weight to find the CG movement. Worked example: an illustrative 2,000 lb airplane has a CG at 40 in. Moving 100 lb from a 60 in arm to a 100 in arm adds 4,000 lb·in of moment. CG moves 4,000 / 2,000 = 2 in aft , to 42 in. Whether 42 in is acceptable depends entirely on that airplane’s approved envelope. For a shift, ΔCG = w × d / W. This shortcut works because the denominator W is unchanged. Adding or removing a load changes both total moment and total weight; recompute both rather than treating it as a shift. Fuel burn is removal of weight at the tank’s arm. If the tanks lie forward of the current CG, burning their fuel moves CG aft; tanks aft of CG tend to produce the opposite change. Tanks, transfer systems, and loading restrictions vary, so check the actual aircraft and planned fuel states. Secure any approved ballast so its effective arm cannot change during turbulence or maneuvering. An illustrative 2,000 lb airplane has 100 lb of baggage moved 40 in aft. Total weight stays constant. subject: Performance and Limitations
title: Why weight and CG change how the airplane flies
text: Performance and Limitations Why weight and CG change how the airplane flies At the same speed and configuration, a heavier airplane needs more lift for level flight. The wing generally operates at a higher angle of attack, leaving less margin to the critical angle. Stall speed increases with the square root of the supported load when configuration and maximum lift coefficient are held fixed. CG changes stability and control authority as well as performance. In many conventional trainers, a forward CG increases the tail force and wing lift needed for trim, potentially increasing stall speed and drag. Excessively forward loading can leave inadequate elevator authority for rotation or flare. An aft CG reduces longitudinal stability and can worsen stall or spin recovery. Common trap: a potentially lower stall speed with an aft CG does not make aft-limit loading safer. The approved envelope protects controllability and recovery as well as cruise efficiency. For a fixed configuration, stall-speed scaling is V S2 / V S1 = √(W 2 / W 1 ) for a 1 g comparison. If weight rises from 2,000 to 2,420 lb, the ratio is √1.21 = 1.10. An illustrative 50 kt reference stall speed becomes 55 kt under the same assumptions. Maneuvering speed also generally decreases with lower weight. V A is not blanket protection from structural damage: abrupt combined-axis, repeated, or alternating inputs can exceed loads even below it. Use the published weight-dependent speeds and limitations. Stability is properly discussed using pitching moments and the neutral point; the wing’s center of pressure is not a fixed pivot from which the CG simply “falls.” A trainer is much lighter than its maximum weight. subject: Performance and Limitations
title: Density altitude connects the atmosphere to performance
text: Performance and Limitations Density altitude connects the atmosphere to performance Pressure altitude expresses pressure relative to the standard atmosphere and can be read approximately by setting a pressure altimeter to 29.92 inHg. Density altitude is pressure altitude adjusted for nonstandard temperature. Heat, lower pressure, and greater elevation generally raise density altitude; humidity also reduces air density. Thin air affects the whole system. A normally aspirated engine takes in less oxygen, the propeller accelerates less mass, and the wing needs a higher true airspeed to achieve the same dynamic pressure. Follow the aircraft’s specified indicated takeoff and approach speeds, but expect higher true airspeed at high density altitude. Wind then determines groundspeed. Apply it: an unchanged runway and familiar indicated rotation speed can still produce a much longer takeoff and weaker climb on a hot afternoon. Evaluate the conditions expected at departure time, not just morning conditions. Dynamic pressure is q = ½ρV². Reducing density ρ while holding indicated-air-speed-related dynamic pressure constant requires true airspeed V to increase. This explains why a familiar indicated approach can carry more groundspeed and kinetic energy in thin air when wind is unchanged. Density altitude is a performance index, not an instruction to add an altitude correction to a flight plan or a universal replacement for chart inputs. If the POH requests pressure altitude and temperature separately, supply those inputs. A pressure-altitude estimate based on field elevation and altimeter setting is an approximation; temperature also affects the relationship between indicated and true altitude. A hot, high airport has no wind. Compared with a low-density-altitude departure at the same weight and configuration, what should a pilot generally expect?

title: Read the conditions before reading the number
text: Performance and Limitations Read the conditions before reading the number Performance tables answer a specific question under specified conditions. Read the title, units, notes, aircraft weight, pressure altitude, temperature, wind convention, runway condition, configuration, and technique before interpolating. Distinguish ground roll from distance over a specified obstacle. For takeoff, check both runway distance and the climb needed beyond the runway. A favorable ground roll does not guarantee terrain clearance. For landing, include the approach and obstacle assumptions rather than comparing runway length only with ground roll. Cruise planning needs time, fuel, and distance for climb and descent as well as cruise. Common trap: copying another trainer’s numbers or extrapolating beyond published chart boundaries. Demonstrate interpolation inside the chart, explain every correction in its notes, and use only approved data applicable to the aircraft and configuration. A 500 ft/min climb means 500 vertical feet per minute. Climb gradient asks how many vertical feet are gained per horizontal mile. At 100 kt groundspeed, 500 ft/min corresponds to 500 × 60 / 100 = 300 ft/NM. At 125 kt groundspeed, the same climb rate yields 240 ft/NM. A tailwind can therefore worsen obstacle-clearance geometry even when vertical climb rate is unchanged. Displayed numbers can look precise while the inputs are uncertain. Ask whether the engine can achieve the charted power, the runway matches the chart condition, and the pilot can consistently achieve the specified technique. If a necessary correction is unavailable, that uncertainty requires a more conservative decision, not invented arithmetic. The POH gives 900 ft ground roll and 1,600 ft over a 50 ft obstacle. subject: Performance and Limitations
title: Make the go/no-go decision before starting the roll
text: Performance and Limitations Make the go/no-go decision before starting the roll Operating limits and personal margins serve different purposes. Approved weight, CG, speed, and configuration limits must be respected. A personal margin then accounts for uncertainty within those limits: wind shifts, surface condition, pilot technique, aircraft condition, and an escape plan. A demonstrated crosswind value records a certification demonstration and is often not itself an operating limitation; verify the actual AFM/POH, placards, supplements, school policy, and pilot proficiency. A charted or approved limitation remains a limitation regardless of the label used in a training note. Apply it: if the plan works only with perfect technique, steady headwind, or optimistic surface assumptions, change the plan. Reduce loading, wait for cooler conditions, choose a different runway or airport, or decline the flight. Decide on aircraft-appropriate abort criteria with your instructor before takeoff. There is no universal 10–20% allowance that makes every takeoff, landing, or fuel plan safe. The appropriate margin depends on the aircraft, available data, environment, operation, and consequences of uncertainty. School or operator policies may require defined margins above legal or published minima. Soft or contaminated surfaces can increase rolling resistance, reduce acceleration, and degrade braking. Never assume grass or softness automatically shortens landing distance. Runway slope, wind, obstacles, and braking conditions must be assessed using applicable data. More indicated airspeed than required can substantially increase landing energy because kinetic energy varies with speed squared; carrying excess speed is not a substitute for a sound margin. subject: National Airspace System
title: Read airspace in three dimensions
text: National Airspace System Read airspace in three dimensions A chart is a plan view of a three-dimensional structure. To identify your airspace, determine the lateral boundary, floor, ceiling, and time of operation. Then compare your altitude with the correct reference: MSL is measured from mean sea level, while AGL is measured above the surface beneath you. Class B shelves use solid blue boundaries and charted MSL floors and ceilings. Class C uses solid magenta, Class D uses dashed blue, and a Class E surface area uses dashed magenta. A magenta vignette commonly marks a 700 ft AGL Class E floor; a blue vignette marks a 1,200 ft AGL floor. It also does not automatically remove an overlapping transponder, ADS-B, speed, or nearby surface-airspace requirement. MSL shelves remain referenced to sea level while the ground rises beneath them, so their height above terrain changes. A 700 ft AGL transition floor follows terrain conceptually rather than describing a constant MSL shelf. The two references answer different questions. Tower closure can change an airport’s surface-airspace classification, but a surrounding transition area does not necessarily disappear. title: Entry rules: clearance is different from contact
text: National Airspace System Entry rules: clearance is different from contact Class Usual entry principle A Normally IFR operation with the required clearance, pilot qualifications, and equipment; generally 18,000 ft MSL through FL600. B Receive an explicit ATC clearance before entry; satisfy pilot and equipment requirements. C or D Establish two-way communications with the responsible ATC facility before entry and maintain them. title: Equipment overlays can extend outside the class boundary
text: National Airspace System Equipment overlays can extend outside the class boundary Transponder and ADS-B Out requirements overlap with airspace classes but do not match them perfectly. For ordinary electrically equipped airplanes, significant ADS-B Out areas include Class B and C, the specified 30 NM Class B airport veil, airspace above Class B/C within their lateral boundaries up to 10,000 ft MSL, and applicable high-altitude Class E. Section 91.225 also contains the coastal Gulf requirement, exceptions, and deviation procedures. At and above 10,000 ft MSL in the contiguous states and DC, the Class E ADS-B requirement excludes airspace at or below 2,500 ft above the surface. Apply the actual rule rather than an unqualified “above ten thousand” slogan. Transponder requirements are separately defined in § 91.215. Common trap: ADS-B In on a tablet is a receiver. It does not satisfy an ADS-B Out transmission requirement and does not show every aircraft. ADS-B is automatic because the equipment broadcasts without a radar interrogation. It is dependent because the report depends on onboard navigation and other aircraft data. A GNSS-derived position is not the same as worldwide delivery of the report: the normal terrestrial radio link and ground reception still have coverage and line-of-sight limits. TIS-B and ADS-R can supplement traffic awareness; FIS-B supplies certain flight information to compatible receivers. Service availability depends on equipment, coverage, and the service involved. A blank traffic display does not establish an empty sky. The see-and-avoid responsibility remains, and datalink weather latency makes it unsuitable for close-range thunderstorm penetration decisions. subject: National Airspace System
title: Speed and separation depend on the operation
text: National Airspace System Speed and separation depend on the operation For ordinary domestic operations, § 91.117 generally limits indicated airspeed below 10,000 ft MSL to 250 kt. At or below 2,500 ft above the surface within 4 NM of a Class C or D primary airport, the usual limit is 200 kt. Beneath a Class B area or in a designated VFR corridor through it, the limit is 200 kt. Read the full rule for the specific authorizations and minimum-safe-airspeed exception. These limits use indicated airspeed, not groundspeed. An ordinary heading, route, or flight-following instruction does not mean the pilot may ignore an applicable speed limit. Controlled airspace also does not mean every VFR aircraft receives the same separation service. Class B separates participating aircraft; Class C includes VFR/IFR separation. Ordinary Class D service does not supply general VFR separation. Continue the appropriate visual scan. Traffic sequencing, traffic information, and separation are related but different services. Being placed behind another airplane in a landing sequence does not remove the pilot’s collision-avoidance responsibilities. Know what the facility is actually providing and clarify instructions when the traffic picture is uncertain. Speed affects the time available to see, decide, and maneuver near a conflict. The same geographic distance disappears faster with a higher closure rate, even though your own indicated speed may appear moderate. Teach students to manage speed and workload early, use radio information to focus their scan, and avoid turning a traffic display into their only source of awareness.

subject: National Airspace System
title: Special VFR is a limited clearance, not a weather escape plan
text: National Airspace System Special VFR is a limited clearance, not a weather escape plan Special VFR allows qualifying operations below basic VFR minimums in certain airport surface areas, with an ATC clearance. For airplanes, the basic special-VFR conditions include remaining clear of clouds and at least 1 SM flight visibility. Takeoff and landing also require at least 1 SM ground visibility when reported, or the specified flight-visibility condition when it is not. It applies within the lateral boundaries of eligible Class B, C, D, or E airport surface areas below 10,000 ft MSL. It does not create a route-wide exemption or authorize an ordinary Class E surface-area extension. Some airports prohibit fixed-wing special VFR. Between sunset and sunrise, the airplane pilot must meet the applicable instrument-flight requirements and the aircraft must have the required IFR equipment. Pilot-specific privileges and limitations still apply. A special-VFR clearance never guarantees obstacle clearance or safe conditions beyond its limits. The clearance solves a traffic-separation problem inside a defined area; it does not solve terrain visibility, deteriorating weather, pilot proficiency, or the transition into surrounding airspace. Before considering it, ask what weather exists along the entire intended route and what legal, safe conditions will exist after leaving the surface area. For a student, do not substitute the 1 SM special-VFR minimum for § 61.89’s higher visibility limits or required visual reference to the surface. Instructor restrictions and endorsements still matter. subject: National Airspace System
title: Special-use airspace and temporary restrictions
text: National Airspace System Special-use airspace and temporary restrictions Restricted and prohibited areas are regulatory. Their legal descriptions and controlling or using agencies matter. Restricted-area activity, scheduling, and authorization determine whether entry is permitted. A prohibited area requires specific authorization; never assume ordinary flight following clears it. MOAs separate military activity from certain other operations. VFR entry is generally possible without a clearance, but high-speed military traffic makes activity status and a conservative routing decision important. Alert and warning areas communicate hazards. Controlled firing areas use monitoring and suspension of activity to protect nonparticipating aircraft, so they are not normally charted like an MOA. Apply it: review current charts, NOTAMs, and authoritative TFR information before flight and update when conditions change. An EFB’s shaded shape can lag or omit details; the actual notice defines location, times, altitudes, exceptions, and contacts. Do not confuse permission with prudence. An inactive restricted area may be available subject to its published provisions, while a legally accessible active MOA can still be an unsuitable place for a basic lesson. Ask the controlling agency for status when appropriate and retain a route that remains acceptable if access is unavailable. Publication currency is also a layered problem. A current sectional does not include every temporary change, and a current database does not guarantee current receiver software or valid operating approval. subject: Navigation Systems and Radar Services
title: VOR radials describe position from a station
text: Navigation Systems and Radar Services VOR radials describe position from a station A VOR supplies angular information referenced to a ground station. A radial is named for the magnetic direction extending from the station. An airplane north of a station is near its 360° radial whether its nose points north, south, or sideways to that line. Tune the correct frequency, verify the received station identifier by the method approved for the installed equipment, and check operational status and signal validity. A stored database label alone may simply identify the station the receiver expects; some equipment actually decodes and verifies the received identifier. Know the difference. VHF reception is limited by line of sight, terrain, altitude, and the facility’s service volume. A needle that happens to center does not make an out-of-service or unusable signal suitable for navigation. Check NOTAMs and the published facility information before depending on it. The course selected with the OBS defines a line through the station. The CDI then shows which side of that selected line the aircraft occupies. TO/FROM distinguishes the appropriate side of the station relative to the selected course. It does not sense the airplane’s heading or report whether it is presently moving toward the station. For an airplane north of the station, selecting 180° centers a suitable indication with TO; selecting 360° centers the same geographic line with FROM. subject: Navigation Systems and Radar Services
title: CDI sensing: establish the course picture before turning
text: Navigation Systems and Radar Services CDI sensing: establish the course picture before turning To track inbound on the north side of a VOR, a pilot would normally select the 180° course with a TO indication, then fly an appropriate intercept heading. To track outbound to the north, select 360° with FROM. In either case, establish the intended course direction and recognize which side of that line the aircraft occupies. A conventional CDI can give reverse-sensing confusion when the airplane is flown opposite the selected course direction. “Turn toward the needle” is unsafe as a universal rule. First build the geometry, select the intended course correctly, and use the instrument according to its design. An HSI helps display that geometry but still requires correct source and course interpretation. Apply it: identify the navigation source as well as the needle. A VOR, localizer, and GPS indication may use the same display while measuring different types of deviation. VOR deviation is angular. The same angular error corresponds to a smaller cross-track distance close to the station and a larger distance far away. That is why a fixed-size correction made near the station can produce a rapidly moving needle and unnecessary oscillation. For a small angular error θ, cross-track distance is approximately station distance multiplied by θ in radians. At a 1° angular error, 60 NM corresponds to about 1 NM lateral displacement; 6 NM corresponds to about 0.1 NM. Those are teaching approximations, not receiver tolerances. Near station passage, rapid angular changes and unreliable indications in the overhead region require anticipation rather than aggressive needle chasing. subject: Navigation Systems and Radar Services
title: DME measures a slanted line, not the map distance
text: Navigation Systems and Radar Services DME measures a slanted line, not the map distance DME interrogates a ground facility and measures the timing of its replies. The displayed distance is the straight-line slant range from aircraft to station, in nautical miles. It is not automatically horizontal distance to the airport or runway. When far from a station and relatively low above it, slant range and horizontal distance are close. Over the station at altitude, the display mainly reflects vertical separation. An airplane about 6,000 ft above the DME antenna will still read about 1 NM when directly overhead. Verify that the distance belongs to the intended, correctly identified facility. Paired VOR/DME channels and combined equipment make tuning convenient, but a familiar-looking distance is not proof that it belongs to the selected airport or localizer. Read the chart and installed-equipment indications. The geometry is a right triangle: slant range² = horizontal distance² + height above station², with all three distances in the same units. Height above station is different from altitude MSL. The station elevation must be considered before comparing vertical separation with a charted altitude. Slant range can also make distance-based groundspeed or time-to-station displays misleading while climbing, descending, or flying across the station rather than directly toward it. A changing distance is a range rate, not necessarily the aircraft’s full groundspeed. subject: Navigation Systems and Radar Services
title: GPS position and GPS integrity are separate questions
text: Navigation Systems and Radar Services GPS position and GPS integrity are separate questions A GNSS receiver uses accurately timed satellite signals to solve for position and receiver-clock error. Four suitable satellites can support a basic three-dimensional position solution. That does not by itself establish that the solution has adequate integrity for an intended operation. RAIM compares redundant measurements to detect inconsistent data. Conventional unaugmented GPS typically needs at least five satellites for fault detection, or four with suitable barometric aiding. Fault detection and exclusion generally needs six, or five with barometric aiding. Satellite geometry matters as well as count. WAAS adds corrections and integrity information through a network of reference stations and broadcast links. It is not simply a fixed number of extra satellites. Read the receiver’s actual status and applicable flight-manual supplement. A handheld moving-map position is useful information, but it does not establish approval for an IFR navigation function. Four unknowns require four independent measurements: three position coordinates and a clock correction. A fifth measurement creates redundancy, allowing a consistency check. Extra satellites can improve redundancy, but a poor geometric arrangement can still weaken the solution; integrity availability is not guaranteed merely by counting icons. GNSS interference, signal blockage, database errors, or an incorrectly selected leg can produce different failure modes. A valid satellite solution can still guide the pilot along the wrong programmed course. Cross-check the intended route against independent information and prepare a practical alternative before a loss of navigation becomes urgent. Perform required RAIM predictions and other preflight checks according to the equipment and operation. title: GPS guidance depends on the active leg and flight phase
text: Navigation Systems and Radar Services GPS guidance depends on the active leg and flight phase A GPS flight plan is a sequence of legs, not merely a list of destinations. Confirm the active leg, its course, the selected navigation source, and whether the receiver is sequencing or holding a leg. “Direct to” can change the route geometry and may bypass intended fixes. GPS lateral deviation generally represents cross-track distance, unlike a VOR’s angular deviation. The full-scale width can change with operating mode and flight phase. Conventional non-WAAS units commonly use ±2 NM en route, ±1 NM in terminal mode, and ±0.3 NM for an eligible nonprecision approach. Those values are not a universal departure rule or a complete description of modern WAAS approach scaling. Apply it: interpret the annunciated mode and the aircraft’s approved equipment documentation. A centered needle without the intended source, leg, and scale can be reassuring for the wrong reason. At a 0.2 NM cross-track error, a wide en-route scale and a narrow approach scale produce very different needle positions, even though the aircraft has not moved. The sensitivity change is intentional: increasingly precise path control is needed as protected airspace and procedure geometry change. Approach authorization also depends on procedure loading, database currency, receiver capability, integrity status, and aircraft approval. For an IFR procedure, manually building an approximation from waypoint coordinates does not replace retrieving the approved named procedure when required. subject: Navigation Systems and Radar Services
title: Flight following helps; it does not take over the flight
text: Navigation Systems and Radar Services Flight following helps; it does not take over the flight Request VFR radar advisories with aircraft identification, type, position, altitude, destination, and the service needed. Availability can depend on controller workload, equipment, coverage, and the airspace involved. A discrete code and traffic advisories do not automatically supply clearance into every airspace along the route. Primary radar can detect reflected energy without a transponder reply. Secondary surveillance uses transponder responses. Mode A provides a code, Mode C adds pressure-altitude reporting, and Mode S supports selective addressing and additional data. ADS-B broadcasts aircraft-derived information rather than waiting for a traditional radar interrogation. The pilot retains responsibility for navigation, fuel, weather avoidance, terrain clearance, and see-and-avoid as applicable. Advise ATC promptly if an instruction conflicts with maintaining VFR. When assigned a heading, fly the assigned heading rather than substituting the same numeric GPS ground track. Controllers see surveillance-derived position and track, but they cannot infer the exact cloud boundary visible out your windshield. Weather displays show selected precipitation information and have limitations; they do not depict all cloud, icing, turbulence, or other hazards. Do not accept a vector into conditions you cannot safely and legally enter. Use traffic information as a cue for an active visual search. Aircraft may be outside coverage, unequipped, unreported, or filtered from a display. A “no traffic” impression is not a guarantee. Read back and comply with applicable ATC instructions, clarify ambiguity early, and understand when advisory service has terminated or a handoff requires action.
