subject: Navigation and Cross-Country Flight Planning
title: Course is the plan; heading is a control input
text: Navigation and Cross-Country Flight Planning Course is the plan; heading is a control input Course is the intended path over the ground. Heading is where the aircraft’s longitudinal axis points. Track is the path actually made over the ground. Wind makes those three directions differ. True airspeed describes motion through the air; groundspeed describes motion across the surface. The airspeed vector and wind vector add to form the groundspeed vector. A crosswind calls for a heading correction into the wind to hold the intended course. A headwind mainly reduces groundspeed, increasing time and fuel for the same distance. Apply it: establish whether a reported wind direction is “from” and whether the source uses true or magnetic reference. E6B or EFB planning should convert the reported wind into a consistent reference frame before solving the wind triangle. A plausible-looking heading can still be wrong if the references were mixed. For a pure 20 kt crosswind and 100 kt true airspeed, holding the desired track requires an into-wind correction of arcsin(20/100), approximately 11.5°. Some of the airspeed vector now cancels crosswind; the along-track groundspeed is approximately √(100² − 20²) = 98 kt. Crab angle is therefore not created by simply subtracting the wind speed from true airspeed. For basic navigation calculations, apply wind to true course to get true heading, then variation to get magnetic heading, then the aircraft’s compass-deviation correction when using the magnetic compass. Check the signs with a sketch or trusted method. A GPS track display helps assess drift but does not eliminate the need to understand the desired ground path.

subject: Navigation and Cross-Country Flight Planning
title: Choose checkpoints that can prove your position
text: Navigation and Cross-Country Flight Planning Choose checkpoints that can prove your position Use current sectional or terminal charts and applicable airport information to build a route around terrain, obstacles, controlled airspace, special-use activity, and practical landing options. A straight line is only the first candidate route. Good visual checkpoints are distinctive, easy to identify from the expected direction, and spaced so a wrong position can be detected early. A uniquely shaped lake, a recognizable road-river crossing, or an airport can work better than a similar-looking town. Choose spacing to match speed, visibility, terrain, and workload; “every 10–15 NM” is a planning suggestion rather than a regulation. Read airport elevation, runway information, obstacles, and chart annotations with the correct units and altitude references. A maximum elevation figure is an area summary, not a route-specific clearance, an IFR minimum altitude, or a guarantee of legal terrain separation. Pilotage identifies position from observed landmarks. Dead reckoning predicts position from heading, groundspeed, and elapsed time. Used together, they expose errors: if the expected landmark does not appear when predicted, either the position, speed, wind, identification, or timing assumption needs review. Charts also simplify information. A landmark can be obscured, a tower can be added between editions, and an EFB layer can be turned off. Review the legend, effective dates, NOTAMs, and terrain along plausible escape routes. Download the needed charts before flight and know which information will remain available after loss of internet, power, or a location signal.

subject: Navigation and Cross-Country Flight Planning
title: Build the time and fuel calculation leg by leg
text: Navigation and Cross-Country Flight Planning Build the time and fuel calculation leg by leg For each leg, identify distance and true course, obtain an appropriate wind forecast, use the aircraft’s expected true airspeed and fuel flow, and calculate heading, groundspeed, time, and fuel. Include climb, cruise, descent, taxi, and other relevant fuel use with the performance data applicable to those phases. Time in minutes equals distance in NM divided by groundspeed in knots, multiplied by 60. Fuel for a phase equals its duration in hours multiplied by the appropriate fuel-flow rate. Keep units visible. A 60 NM leg at 90 kt takes 40 minutes, not one hour; at 9 gal/hr, that cruise segment uses 6 gal. Apply it: make a nav log that the pilot can actually use. Record expected checkpoint times and fuel states, then compare them with the flight rather than treating the finished worksheet as an administrative exercise. An EFB automates arithmetic, not truth. Aircraft identity, usable fuel, loading, power setting, fuel flow, departure time, altitude, and wind data all influence the output. A default performance profile can turn optimistic inputs into highly precise-looking errors. Verify representative results against the POH and observed aircraft performance. In flight, recompute groundspeed from a known distance and elapsed time. If 30 NM took 24 minutes, groundspeed was 75 kt. A forecast 90 kt groundspeed for the next 60 NM would predict 40 minutes; continuing at 75 kt would take 48 minutes. This is why unexpected headwind must change fuel and diversion decisions before the reserve becomes small. A known 60 NM cruise leg is planned at 90 kt groundspeed and 9 gal/hr. subject: Navigation and Cross-Country Flight Planning
title: Choose an altitude for the whole route
text: Navigation and Cross-Country Flight Planning Choose an altitude for the whole route Altitude selection must satisfy terrain and obstacle clearance, airspace, weather, aircraft climb capability, navigation coverage, pilot limits, and fuel efficiency. A favorable wind is useful only if the airplane can reach and safely use that altitude. Under the ordinary § 91.159 rule, VFR level cruising flight more than 3,000 ft above the surface uses the magnetic course : 000°–179° calls for odd thousands plus 500 ft MSL, and 180°–359° calls for even thousands plus 500 ft MSL below 18,000 ft MSL. The regulation contains exceptions and ATC authorization provisions. Do not select the side of the rule from heading or GPS true track. Apply it: a wind-corrected heading of 175° does not control the rule when the magnetic course is 185°. The course points to the even-thousand-plus-500 side. The height trigger uses the surface below you; the selected cruising altitude uses MSL. Over rising terrain, one constant MSL altitude can move closer to the ground. Reassess terrain clearance and the applicability of the cruising-altitude rule along the route rather than only at departure. Plan descent as deliberately as climb. The common 3 NM per 1,000 ft descent estimate describes an approximate geometric path, not a guaranteed descent performance or a universal procedure. Required vertical speed depends on groundspeed, desired path, configuration, and aircraft limits. Begin early enough to manage airspace, temperatures, airspeed, traffic, and arrival workload without a rushed descent. subject: Navigation and Cross-Country Flight Planning
title: Legal reserve is the floor of the plan
text: Navigation and Cross-Country Flight Planning Legal reserve is the floor of the plan For a VFR airplane flight, § 91.151 requires enough fuel at departure, considering wind and forecast weather, to reach the first intended landing point and then continue at normal cruising speed for at least 30 minutes by day or 45 minutes at night. Use usable fuel, not the total capacity printed on a tank placard. The legal planning minimum is not a target for how little fuel should remain at landing. Add the fuel needed for realistic delays, climb, diversions, weather uncertainty, and the operator’s or pilot’s chosen reserve. Establish an early decision point for an unplanned fuel stop. Worked example: for an illustrative constant 10 gal/hr flight lasting 90 minutes, with no additional taxi fuel in this simplified calculation, the trip uses 15 gal. Adding the daytime 30-minute reserve adds 5 gal, giving a 20 gal regulatory planning baseline. A percentage contingency and a time reserve solve different problems. Ten percent extra cruise fuel may be only a few minutes on a short trip, while a long headwind leg can consume a large amount of fuel before the error is recognized. Express the actual fuel state both as gallons and as remaining time at a defensible flow rate. Fuel exhaustion means the usable supply has been depleted. Fuel starvation means fuel is not reaching the engine despite fuel remaining somewhere in the aircraft. Tank selection, imbalance, venting, pumps, and aircraft procedures matter. A large calculated reserve cannot protect against an incorrectly selected tank or an inaccurate starting-fuel assumption. subject: Navigation and Cross-Country Flight Planning
title: Brief the weather and preserve a usable alternative
text: Navigation and Cross-Country Flight Planning Brief the weather and preserve a usable alternative Preflight information must support the proposed operation. Review current and forecast weather, NOTAMs, TFRs, airport conditions, delays, runway lengths, available alternatives, and aircraft performance. Use § 91.103 to understand the applicable preflight duty rather than treating a mnemonic as the entire rule. Ask what will make the plan unacceptable, when that change can be recognized, and where to land if it occurs. Set limits before departure, when there is time to think clearly. A usable alternative must fit weather, fuel, runway, terrain, opening hours, and the aircraft’s equipment. A VFR flight plan supports search-and-rescue processes. It does not provide an ATC clearance or automatically start flight following. Arrange activation and closure by an appropriate available method, and update the plan when the route or destination changes. Separate a forecast from an observation and compare both with trends. A departure airport reporting good conditions does not establish the route, pass, or destination will remain suitable at arrival. Consider ceilings, visibility, winds, convection, icing exposure, density altitude, and daylight relevant to the actual flight. External pressure can make an unsafe plan look attractive: an instructor appointment, passengers, a return commitment, or the desire to finish a cross-country requirement. Build alternatives that remove that pressure, such as a different day, a fuel stop, a shorter route, or ground transport. subject: Navigation and Cross-Country Flight Planning
title: Divert early; ask for help before uncertainty grows
text: Navigation and Cross-Country Flight Planning Divert early; ask for help before uncertainty grows When the planned destination or route becomes unsuitable, select a realistic alternative while there is still time and fuel. Establish a safe heading, estimate distance and groundspeed, calculate time and fuel, assess terrain and airspace, obtain airport and weather information, and refine the plan as workload permits. If position is uncertain, keep aircraft control first. Use reliable landmarks, a second navigation source, or ATC/Flight Service assistance. A climb may improve visibility or radio reception only when weather, terrain, airspace, and aircraft performance permit it. A memorized “climb” step is not authority to enter cloud or violate an airspace boundary. Apply it: communicate the actual problem plainly. If the situation is urgent, use appropriate urgency or distress language rather than delaying help to avoid embarrassment. Declare an emergency when warranted. A good diversion estimate is intentionally coarse at first. At 90 kt groundspeed, 15 NM takes about 10 minutes; at a 9 gal/hr flow, that segment consumes about 1.5 gal before approach and other allowances. A quick estimate identifies whether an option is plausible while a detailed calculation can follow. The trap is persisting with a detailed electronic setup while the airplane flies farther from the safe option. Reduce workload, share tasks appropriately, and maintain a visual flight path. subject: 14 CFR and Publications
title: Start with the question, then choose the rule
text: 14 CFR and Publications Start with the question, then choose the rule A pilot does not need to memorize every paragraph, but must recognize the controlling source and find the applicable text accurately. 14 CFR Part 1 supplies definitions. Part 61 addresses pilot and instructor certificates, ratings, privileges, training, endorsements, experience, and logging. Part 91 contains general aircraft operating rules. NTSB accident and incident reporting is in 49 CFR Part 830 , not 14 CFR. Separate the person from the operation. A pilot can hold the right certificate but lack required recent experience. A current pilot can still be in an aircraft that lacks required equipment or inspections. An aircraft can be airworthy but unsuitable for the weather or planned route. Apply it: “May I act as PIC?” and “May I log PIC?” are different questions. Find the rule that matches the precise action, pilot qualifications, aircraft, and circumstances. Definitions determine scope. When a rule uses terms such as category, class, night, or flight time, look up the applicable definition and any rule-specific qualification before relying on an everyday meaning. A familiar word can have different significance in aircraft certification, airman certification, or a particular operating requirement. Read the surrounding paragraph, exceptions, and cross-references. A search-result snippet may omit the condition that changes the answer. Explain the reasoning as “This operation has these facts; this paragraph applies because of those facts; these conditions remain to be met.” That produces a more durable answer than memorizing a yes/no conclusion from a different scenario. subject: 14 CFR and Publications
title: Regulations and guidance answer different questions
text: 14 CFR and Publications Regulations and guidance answer different questions Regulations establish requirements. Approved aircraft operating limitations, markings, and placards must also be followed under § 91.9. The AIM explains flight information and ATC procedures; advisory circulars, handbooks, safety alerts, and similar guidance help explain methods and risks. Guidance is generally not a separate regulation. An advisory circular can describe an acceptable way to comply without making every sentence an independent legal command. Conversely, calling something “advisory” does not excuse disregarding an actual rule, approved limitation, clearance, or incorporated requirement that applies to the operation. Apply it: when a training note says “required,” identify the source of that requirement. Is it regulation, an approved aircraft limitation, an instructor endorsement restriction, operator policy, or recommended practice? All can influence your decision, but their authority and scope differ. Use guidance to understand the rationale and a sound compliance method, then connect it back to the governing requirement. If a regulation incorporates material by reference, that incorporated requirement can have legal significance that a generic statement about advisory material misses. FAA Chief Counsel interpretations explain how the agency reads particular provisions and facts. They are important research material, but are not new regulations or a substitute for reading the present rule. An old interpretation can address a superseded rule or different facts. Check date, applicability, later amendments, and whether the interpretation has been superseded rather than treating every letter as a universal binding answer. subject: 14 CFR and Publications
title: The aircraft’s approved information controls the aircraft
text: 14 CFR and Publications The aircraft’s approved information controls the aircraft The AFM/POH and its approved supplements describe the aircraft’s limitations, normal and emergency procedures, performance, systems, and other required information. Use the documents applicable to the actual aircraft, installed equipment, and configuration. Some POHs contain FAA-approved material as well as other manufacturer information; know how the manual identifies each. subject: Night Operations
title: Why off-center viewing works
text: Night Operations Why off-center viewing works Cones support detailed color vision in brighter light and are concentrated near the center of the retina. Rods are much more useful in dim conditions but do not provide color information. The central visual area has few rods, so a faint object may become easier to detect when you look slightly beside it rather than staring directly at it. Dark adaptation takes time, often roughly 30 minutes for substantial adaptation. Bright light can rapidly spoil it. Dim cockpit lighting to the lowest level that still makes instruments, switches, and charts readable. Red light can help preserve adaptation, but it changes color appearance and can hide chart details; carefully controlled white light remains useful for identification and inspection. Why: A darker cockpit is helpful only if you can still read what matters. Fatigue, smoking, illness, and reduced oxygen availability can degrade visual performance even when the outside air looks clear. title: One airplane, two altitude environments
text: Pressurization One airplane, two altitude environments Aircraft altitude describes the airplane’s position in the atmosphere. Cabin pressure altitude describes the pressure experienced by its occupants. A pressurized airplane can therefore fly at a high flight level while maintaining a much lower cabin altitude. Three cabin indications answer different questions: cabin altitude shows the present pressure environment, cabin rate shows how rapidly it is changing, and differential pressure shows the inside-to-outside pressure difference. title: Control the air leaving the cabin
text: Pressurization Control the air leaving the cabin A typical system supplies compressed air and meters its escape through an outflow valve. Restricting outflow tends to raise cabin pressure and lower cabin altitude, provided enough air is entering. Increasing outflow tends to reduce cabin pressure. The controller commands the valve according to the selected or programmed cabin schedule. The safety functions are distinct. Positive-pressure relief protects against excessive inside-to-outside pressure difference. title: Gradual and rapid failures need early recognition
text: Pressurization Gradual and rapid failures need early recognition A gradual failure may have little noise or physical sensation. Its danger is that the cabin altitude can increase while the pilot’s judgment deteriorates. A rapid decompression may produce a loud event, cooling, fog, airflow, and sudden physiological exposure. The severity depends on aircraft altitude, cabin volume, opening size, and other conditions. Preserve breathing and aircraft control immediately, then execute the aircraft-specific emergency procedure. That generally includes prompt use of appropriate oxygen and an emergency descent when required, coordinated with terrain, traffic, and structural or speed limitations. Treat the aircraft checklist and training as the authority for configuration and sequence. Why: Useful decision time shrinks sharply at high cabin altitudes, and rapid decompression can reduce it further. An oxygen mask buried in a bag is not functionally ready. Practice locating and operating the actual equipment while on the ground. Brief passengers and assign crew tasks before flight so that recognition does not have to be followed by an improvised discussion. Why is gradual pressurization loss especially insidious?

title: Additional oxygen protection at high flight levels
text: Pressurization Additional oxygen protection at high flight levels For a pressurized aircraft, §91.211(b) adds requirements based on aircraft flight altitude . Above FL250, provide each occupant at least a ten-minute emergency oxygen supply in addition to oxygen otherwise required by the general cabin-altitude rule. Above FL350, the ordinary rule requires a pilot at the controls to wear and use the specified oxygen mask. The two-pilot quick-donning exception applies at or below FL410 when both pilots are at the controls and each has a qualifying mask that can be donned with one hand within five seconds, secured, sealed, and delivering oxygen. Above FL350, if one pilot leaves the controls, the remaining pilot must use a mask until the other returns. Apply it: A normal low cabin altitude does not remove the emergency-supply requirement above FL250. The high-flight-level rule prepares for the cabin that could exist after a failure, while the general rule addresses the current cabin environment. These are layered protections. title: Qualification follows aircraft capability
text: Pressurization Qualification follows aircraft capability Section 61.31(g) establishes additional training and endorsement requirements for acting as PIC of the defined high-altitude pressurized aircraft. Its capability test uses the lower of service ceiling and maximum operating altitude: that value must be above 25,000 feet MSL. Do not decide applicability solely from today’s planned cruise altitude. The ordinary pathway includes documented ground training in physiology, high-altitude conditions, decompression, and related subjects, plus flight training and a proficiency endorsement. The flight portion covers high-altitude cruise, a simulated rapid-decompression response without actually depressurizing the aircraft, and emergency descent procedures. Review the rule’s documented exceptions before concluding that new training is required. Apply it: Planning to fly a qualifying airplane only at 18,000 feet does not itself remove the qualification requirement. The aircraft-capability rule and the oxygen operating rule answer different questions. This lesson supplies conceptual preparation; it does not issue an endorsement or replace the required aircraft or approved-device training and instructor determination.

subject: Pressurization
title: Why decompression changes more than oxygen
text: Pressurization Why decompression changes more than oxygen At a given temperature, a trapped gas tends to expand as surrounding pressure falls. A decompression can therefore affect ears, sinuses, and other gas spaces while simultaneously reducing oxygen availability. Cabin temperature may drop, and visible condensation can appear as the air expands and cools. Neither fog nor its absence alone describes the full severity of the event. The pressure vessel also carries mechanical load. For a simplified panel, force equals differential pressure multiplied by area. A modest pressure difference across a large area creates a substantial force, which is why relief functions and operating limitations matter. Actual fuselage stresses and door behavior depend on structure and design. Deeper connection: Boyle’s-law reasoning, pV approximately constant for a fixed gas amount at constant temperature, helps explain trapped-gas expansion. It is a teaching approximation for a gas pocket, not a complete transient model of a leaking, cooling cabin. Use it to explain the direction of change while relying on the aircraft design and AFM/POH for actual limitations and responses. text: Steep Turns Why bank costs lift, stall margin, and power. Tilting the lift vector makes the turn. Increasing its magnitude keeps the airplane level. Bank redirects some lift horizontally. If total lift stayed equal to weight, its vertical component would shrink and the airplane would descend. Level flight therefore requires more total lift. At the same speed, that means more angle of attack and more induced drag. At 60° bank, lift doubles and the induced-drag term quadruples. Total drag does not necessarily quadruple. Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor. Bank alone does not create that load: the relationship assumes a coordinated, constant-altitude turn. title: Power-On / Power-Off Stalls
text: Power-On / Power-Off Stalls Same critical angle. Different energy and control effects. A stall is an angle-of-attack limit. Airspeed is only one way to arrive there. Angle of attack is measured between the wing’s chord and the relative airflow, not the horizon. Beyond the critical angle, separation reduces lift and increases drag. Published stall speed describes a particular weight, load factor, and configuration. Increase the demanded lift and the same wing reaches its critical angle at a higher speed. Power changes thrust, slipstream, pitch requirements, and yawing tendencies. It can change the actual stall speed and cues, but it does not remove the critical-angle limit. Both stall types belong in the same lesson. text: Power-Off 180 Track the energy you exchange and the energy you lose. Pitch redistributes energy between height and speed. Drag removes it from both accounts. In a power-off approach, descent does not convert all potential energy into speed: drag continuously removes mechanical energy. At constant airspeed, kinetic energy stays constant while altitude pays the drag bill. Slowing releases kinetic energy; accelerating spends more altitude. Neither exchange replaces energy lost to drag. “Stretching” a glide can increase angle of attack and induced drag. Flaps alter lift, drag, and trim. Here, extra flap drag steepens the energy loss. Ground effect reduces induced drag near the surface, so excess speed may dissipate more slowly and produce a longer float. It supplies no new energy. subject: Maneuvers
title: Eights on Pylons
text: Eights on Pylons Derive pivotal altitude instead of memorizing the divisor. Pivotal altitude is the height where the sight-line geometry matches the turning geometry. The pylon must remain along a sight line parallel to the airplane’s lateral axis. In an ideal coordinated circle, bank fixes the slope of that line; turning acceleration fixes the circle’s radius. Eliminate the radius and bank disappears. Speed remains squared. A 10% increase in speed therefore requires about 21% more pivotal height. The FAA’s operational estimate uses groundspeed, so the required height changes around the maneuver as the wind changes groundspeed. It is height above the pylon’s elevation; add that elevation to obtain MSL altitude. Start with a steady, coordinated, level circle in still air. V is both true airspeed and groundspeed in this ideal case. L cos ⁡ φ = m g L sin ⁡ φ = m V 2 R tan ⁡ φ = V 2 g R The lateral sight line is tilted down by bank φ. subject: Maneuvers
title: Dutch Rolls
text: Dutch Rolls Separate roll–yaw coupling from the coordination exercise. The natural Dutch-roll mode is a coupled oscillation. The trainer exercise is deliberate control coordination. Natural mode: a sideslip creates rolling response through dihedral effect and a yawing response through directional stability. Inertia and phase differences can carry the airplane past equilibrium, producing coupled oscillation. Damping determines how quickly it settles. Weak damping prolongs sideslip, lateral acceleration, and rolling motion, degrading ride and making precise control harder. A yaw damper adds damping through rudder feedback; actual behavior depends on the aircraft. Coordination exercise: alternating bank while holding a visual heading reference practices aileron–rudder timing. Aileron-induced adverse yaw is one reason coordination matters. This is not the same as deliberately exciting the natural mode. A real lateral-directional model couples sideslip β, roll rate p, yaw rate r, and bank φ. title: Turns Around a Point
text: Turns Around a Point Why a constant ground radius needs a changing bank. The ground track is a circle. The air-relative velocity generally is not tangent to that circle. Wind adds a velocity vector. Maintaining a circular ground track therefore needs both a changing heading correction and a changing bank. For the same ground radius, faster groundspeed requires more normal acceleration. The bank is steepest near the downwind part and shallowest near the upwind part. A constant bank approximately draws a circle through the air mass, not a circle fixed to the ground. Constant bank with wind produces a drifting ground track. In still air, coordinated level-turn force balance gives: tan ⁡ φ = V 2 g R With steady uniform wind, ground and air accelerations are equal, but their velocities differ. Let δ be the angle between heading and ground track. Project the air-normal acceleration onto the ground-track normal: a g , ⊥ = g tan ⁡ φ cos ⁡ δ = V g 2 R tan ⁡ φ = V g 2 g R cos ⁡ δ Resolve wind into along-track Wt and cross-track Wn components, holding true airspeed Va constant: V g = W t + V a 2 − W n 2 cos ⁡ δ = V a 2 − W n 2 V a The familiar groundspeed-squared relation captures the main effect. The cos δ term includes the heading–track geometry. Add wind and scrub around the circle. The heading arrow changes relative to the track, and the required bank changes even though the radius does not.
